drills.q: A team trims whitespace and casts a couple of obviously-messy columns to the right type in bronze because 'it's harmless.' Why does this violate the bronze contract, and what does it cost you later?
drills.a: Bronze's contract is to be a faithful, complete copy of what the source sent. Once any cleaning happens there, you can no longer distinguish a source bug from a transformation bug during an incident, and you've lost the ability to prove what the source actually sent versus what your pipeline did to it.

drills.q: A gold-layer query joins fact_orders directly to bronze.customers_raw to save a step, skipping silver's conforming logic. Two months later a second gold mart does the same join differently. What goes wrong, and why?
drills.a: Each gold mart re-derives its own definition of 'customer' from raw data instead of reading one conformed entity from silver, so the two marts can disagree on customer counts or attributes. This is exactly the failure the layering exists to prevent — gold should only read from silver's conformed tables (or other gold objects), never bronze directly.

drills.q: Why must the grain of a gold fact table be decided and documented before any transformation logic from silver to gold is written?
drills.a: Every join, aggregation, and SCD choice downstream assumes a fixed grain. Discovering the grain was wrong (too coarse) after several teams have already built consumers on top of the gold mart is closer to a rebuild than a migration, because you can't disaggregate history you never captured at the finer grain.

drills.q: A fast-growing 40-person startup with 3 source systems is deciding between Kimball, Inmon, and Data Vault for their first warehouse. What's the honest recommendation and why?
drills.a: Kimball, built bottom-up as dimensional marts directly. With few sources and no governance mandate, time-to-value matters most, and Inmon's normalized-EDW-first approach or Data Vault's hub/link/satellite modeling overhead isn't justified by problems (many sources, heavy audit requirements) the startup doesn't actually have yet.

drills.q: A regulated bank integrating 20 source systems asks whether to build Kimball marts directly on raw ingested data, or introduce an integration layer first. What's the tradeoff, and what's the honest hybrid answer?
drills.a: Building Kimball marts directly on raw data skips governance/historization/audit needed at that scale and creates the conform-independently problem across 20 sources. The hybrid answer: a Data Vault or Inmon-style normalized integration core handles historization and governance across all 20 sources, with Kimball-shaped marts built on top of that core specifically for BI consumption — different methodologies solving different layers' constraints.

drills.q: A fact table references a customer_id that hasn't been loaded into dim_customer yet because the fact and dimension pipelines run on different schedules. What happens without handling, and what's the standard fix?
drills.a: Without handling, the fact row either gets dropped (data loss) or its foreign key is left dangling (breaks downstream joins). Standard fix: insert an inferred-member placeholder row in dim_customer with the natural key and a new surrogate key populated, other attributes null, then update it in place as a Type 1 correction when the real dimension data arrives.

drills.q: After a routine dimension refresh, a gold fact table's row count triples with no change in the underlying business activity. Diagnose the bug and give the fix, including why the fix should live in silver rather than every gold query.
drills.a: The gold join matched a Type 2 dimension on natural key with no as-of/effective-date filter, so each fact row matched every historical version of that dimension entity (e.g. 3 address versions = 3x rows). Fix: resolve the correct surrogate key as-of the fact's event date in silver, before the gold join — putting it in silver makes every downstream gold query structurally safe by construction rather than depending on every author remembering to add an as-of filter.

drills.q: A company merges two customer databases from an acquisition. Describe how bronze, silver, and gold each handle this, focusing on what happens to pre-merger historical facts.
drills.a: Bronze lands both companies' raw customer tables unmodified with a source-system tag. Silver resolves both to one conformed natural key via entity resolution (email/phone match or fuzzy matching), with Type 2 SCD so historical facts still join to the pre-merger version of each customer. Pre-merger fact rows are never rewritten — they keep referencing whatever surrogate key was correct in their own timeline, resolved through the silver mapping table at query/gold-build time.

drills.q: Why is generating surrogate keys in bronze, before deduplication, a costly mistake?
drills.a: Bronze can contain multiple raw records representing the same logical entity (duplicate CDC events, or the same customer from two source systems before conforming). Assigning surrogate keys before that resolution happens creates distinct keys for what should be one entity, and once fact tables reference those keys, every dependent fact row's foreign key needs remapping to fix it — expensive to unwind after the fact.

drills.q: Why is deliberate denormalization considered safe in a gold mart but a known anti-pattern in an OLTP schema, and name one case where it's still a real cost even in gold?
drills.a: OLTP schemas are point-updated by application code constantly, so denormalization's update anomalies are a frequent correctness risk; gold is read-heavy and rebuilt/merged on a schedule, so that cost mostly disappears. It's still a real cost in gold when a denormalized attribute changes frequently at high volume (e.g. a flattened segment column touching millions of rows on every update) — the justification holds for read-mostly, infrequently-changing attributes, less so for rapidly mutating ones.
